hints: Recall how solubility of Group 2 hydroxides changes from Mg(OH)2 used as a suspension to Ba(OH)2 used as a solution.
walkthrough:
Picture the familiar hydroxides**
Think of magnesium hydroxide at the top. It is almost insoluble, that is why it can be used as milk of magnesia suspension. Barium hydroxide near the bottom is much more soluble and forms a strongly alkaline solution. So solubility clearly rises going down.
Final answer: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group.

hints: Compare the states in reaction 1, BaO(s) going to Ba(OH)2(aq), and think what you would see as a solid forms an aqueous solution.
walkthrough:
Read the state symbols**
Reaction 1 shows $\text{BaO(s)}$ reacting with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O(l)}$ to give $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}\text{(aq)}$. You start with a white solid oxide and end with a solution. The visible change is the solid disappearing as it dissolves.
Final answer: White solid disappears / dissolves to form a colourless solution.

hints: Look at reaction 2, Ba(OH)2(aq) to BaCO3(s) + H2O(l), and ask which common gas combines with a hydroxide to make a carbonate plus water.
walkthrough:
Balance atoms in your head**
You have $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ turning into $\text{BaCO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. The extra carbon and extra oxygen to make carbonate must come from somewhere. Hydroxides absorb acidic carbon dioxide from air to form carbonates: $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2} + \text{CO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Think of reaction 3 as a strong base neutralised by ethanoic acid, the barium salt formed will contain the ethanoate anion.
walkthrough:
Apply the base plus acid pattern**
$\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ is a base, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ is an acid. They neutralise to salt plus water: $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2} + 2\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{Ba(CH}_{3}\text{COO)}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. So A is barium ethanoate, $\text{Ba(CH}_{3}\text{COO)}_{2}$.

hints: Recall the general reaction of a Group 2 metal with water gives a metal hydroxide plus hydrogen, then balance Ba, O and H.
walkthrough:
Write the skeleton then balance**
Barium is oxidised by water: $\text{Ba} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}$. You need two $\text{OH}$ groups, so you need two waters. That also gives two $\text{H}_{2}$ units on the left, matching $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}$ on the right. The balanced equation is $$\text{Ba} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}$$

hints: Recall whether Group 2 carbonates become more or less stable to heat on going down the group from Ca to Ba.
walkthrough:
Link stability to position**
Thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, so it distorts the carbonate ion more easily and $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ needs less heat to decompose. Therefore $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ decomposes first.
Final answer: $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ decomposes first because thermal stability of carbonates increases down the group.

hints: Think of each carbonate unit decomposing to its oxide plus CO2, then apply this to both carbonate groups in BaCa(CO3)2.
walkthrough:
Decompose both carbonates together**
Each $\text{MCO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_{2}$. Barytocalcite contains one $\text{BaCO}_{3}$ and one $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ combined as $\text{BaCa(CO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$. Complete decomposition gives both oxides plus two carbon dioxides: $$\text{BaCa(CO}_{3}\text{)}_{2} \rightarrow \text{BaO} + \text{CaO} + 2\text{CO}_{2}$$

hints: Identify the two hydrolysable groups in B, the methyl ester CO2CH3 and the nitrile CN, and recall both give carboxylate salts with hot Ba(OH)2.
Think what acidification with HNO3 does to carboxylate salts, and what small alcohol is released from the CO2CH3 part.
Count the carbon skeleton of B to build the diacid, the chain plus the methyl branch gives a 5 carbon framework with two COOH groups.
walkthrough:
Spot the two functional groups**
Draw out B: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(CN)CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. On the right you have a methyl ester, on the middle carbon you have a nitrile $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. Hot $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ hydrolyses both. The ester gives a carboxylate plus $\text{CH}_{3}\text{O}^{-}$, the nitrile gives a carboxylate plus ammonia.

Follow with acidification**
Adding $\text{HNO}_{3}$ protonates all carboxylates to free carboxylic acids. The $\text{CH}_{3}\text{O}^{-}$ becomes $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$, methanol. That is organic product 1.

Build the diacid skeleton**
The rest of the molecule keeps its carbon framework: $\text{HOOC-CH}_{2}-\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)-COOH}$. This is 2-methylbutanedioic acid, with one $\text{COOH}$ from the original ester end and one $\text{COOH}$ from the original nitrile carbon. Check each carbon has four bonds, both $\text{COOH}$ groups are drawn fully, and the methyl branch is on the carbon next to a $\text{COOH}$. That is organic product 2.

Final answer: Organic product 1: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ / methanol
Organic product 2: $\text{HOOCCH}_{2}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)COOH}$ / 2-methylbutanedioic acid, containing the $\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}$ skeleton with both $\text{COOH}$ groups present.
